questions.q: Which trait makes a workload well-suited to a GPU?
options: Low arithmetic intensity with heavy branching
High arithmetic intensity with large, independent, repeatable operations
A small number of elements processed once
Frequent file I/O and network calls
questions.explain: GPUs excel at workloads with high arithmetic intensity (many FLOPs per byte moved) applied independently across large amounts of data.

questions.q: Why can a very small workload actually run slower on a GPU than on a CPU?
options: GPUs cannot process small amounts of data
The fixed overhead of kernel launch and data transfer can dominate the total time when the actual compute is tiny
Small workloads always exceed GPU memory limits
CPUs have higher clock speeds in all cases
questions.explain: Launching a GPU kernel and transferring data across PCIe both have a fixed cost. For very small workloads, that overhead can exceed the time the GPU would save, making a CPU faster overall.

questions.q: In a typical PyTorch training loop, what usually runs on the CPU rather than the GPU?
options: The forward pass through the model
The backward pass computing gradients
The DataLoader's work: reading files, applying augmentations, and batching
The optimizer's parameter update step
questions.explain: DataLoader work such as file I/O, data augmentation, and collation is deliberately kept on the CPU (often across worker processes), while tensor operations after .to("cuda") run on the GPU.

questions.q: What happens if you try to run an operation combining a tensor on the CPU and a tensor on the GPU?
options: PyTorch automatically moves one tensor to match the other silently
The operation runs successfully but slower
A RuntimeError is raised at the first operation touching both tensors
The GPU tensor is silently converted back to CPU
questions.explain: PyTorch does not automatically reconcile device mismatches — combining tensors on different devices raises a RuntimeError at the point they're used together.

questions.q: What does "amortizing overhead" mean in the context of GPU workloads?
options: Reducing the precision of all computations
Spreading a fixed cost, like kernel launch or data transfer, across enough actual work that it stops being significant
Running the same kernel twice to average timing results
Disabling the GPU's memory cache
questions.explain: Amortizing overhead means ensuring there's enough actual compute work that fixed costs like kernel launch and data transfer become a small fraction of total time.
